title: I made 2 games, one with AI Art and one without AI Art. Here are the stats.
author: Curious-Needle
selftext:
So I made 2 games of the same genre and price.

The games are [Idle Reincarnator](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3779340/Idle_Reincarnator/) (IR), a game with AI Art, and [Cradle of the Dark Brood](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4745450/Cradle_of_the_Dark_Brood/) (CotDB), a game without AI Art.

I'll be doing a comparison between the two of them. The stats compared will be Wishlists, Sales, Playtime, and Ratings. TLDR at the bottom.

**Wishlists**

Previously, I made a post comparing their wishlists from when their store page were created.

https://preview.redd.it/ormcnw7nlt8h1.png?width=1000&format=png&auto=webp&s=61e3eaec3e65910ba0cff1ca37503746148df6f3

As you can see the game with IR significantly has more wishlist (1997) compared to CotDB (214) . The reason for this might be that IR has better capsule art compared to CotDB and that IR already has fans previously. Below is their capsules for reference

https://preview.redd.it/ntzn6sb7ot8h1.png?width=382&format=png&auto=webp&s=922f2a87fa4c8fb2700e51e9aff786c983ccfef8

https://preview.redd.it/vrd9yekbot8h1.png?width=376&format=png&auto=webp&s=92f472e191328182b287f765be91410c6df386eb

**Sales**

Now let's compared their sales. To make things as fair as possible, I'll only compare the sales after 1 week after release.

https://preview.redd.it/psalk5a1ot8h1.png?width=800&format=png&auto=webp&s=3928ca703c3e4160e49064c9c96907c715277f84

As you can see, both IR and CotDB almost have similar sales (1153 vs 1078) despite having a large difference in wishlists  (1997 vs 214). I attribute this to Steam creating Personal Calendar which boosted the sales of CotDB and thus almost rivaling IR in terms of sales. Another thing I did was make an announcement on IR's store page about CotDB saying that CotDB is released and thus bringing IR players over to CotDB's page.

**Playtime Metrics and Ratings**

For the playtime metrics, here are the stats.

https://preview.redd.it/fgju35z0kt8h1.png?width=902&format=png&auto=webp&s=7adfe3476b72c03bf53bcec26b300e4bf8290042

CotDB has almost twice the amount of playtime (10h 46min) compared to IR (5h 50min). This might just be because I got better at making games and know what's fun for players. It's hard to say whether it's about AI art.

However, the big difference is in the ratings.

|Game|Ratings|
|:-|:-|
|Idle Reincarnator|98 Reviews -> 68% (Mixed)|
|Cradle of the Dark Brood|23 Reviews -> 91% (Positive)|

CotDB has a significantly better ratings than IR. Looking at the reviews, it might be because IR's name doesn't fit its gameplay.

**TLDR:**

* The game with AI art (Idle Reincarnator) got a lot more wishlists in 21 days than the game without AI art (Cradle of the Dark Brood). (1997 vs 214)
* Despite the large wishlist difference, the game with AI art and the game without AI art almost had the same number of sales. (1153 vs 1078)
* The game without AI art has a higher review score and longer average playtime than the game with AI art.
* Do note that this does not prove that AI art caused the differences. The games also had different gameplay, store presentation, audiences, Steam exposure, and release circumstances.

So yeah do what you will with the data. Feel free to share your thoughts below too.

replies.author: JohannIngvarson
replies.body:
If you have at least a mid range local setup ( I do it with a 3060 12gb and 16gb ddr5), going local with comfyUI workflows is the best thing probably. If you look at complicated ones it'll appear daunting but it's actually quite simple i and you don't need all the bells and whistles.

replies.author: JohannIngvarson
replies.body:
For youtube channels I recommend one called AI Search. He's got a full tutorial on generating images on comfy. 

No you dont use a LLM for this. A stable diffusion model is a seaparate thing. A very common type of model are illustrious based ones. They are variations of the Illustrious model. For these you use tags instead of natural language. 

So instead of "an image of a man sitting by a window in a rainy night" you'd have something like "1boy, mature man, short hair, green eyes, sitting, next to window, rain" as the core. Then there's quality tags and tags for camera positions, etc. And you can increase the weight of a tag by adding () or decrease with []. So lets say you added "muscular" but its not quite enough. You could use ((muscular)), and keep adding parentheses till its enough. You can also do (muscular: 1.5) or (muscular: 0.6) to control weight.

These tags come from a site called Danboruu. So sometimes to check if a tag exists you can look it up there.

There are natural language  models too, like Flux, ZImage, Anima. Some are mixed. Those last two may be mixed. 

Then there are LoRAs. They are kinda like a course adjusment along the way. So for characters, visual styles, lighting methods, etc, you can use LoRAs for consitency. Some characters are well known enough that they'll have tags as default. But lets say you want visible brushstrokes in your image. If prompting isnt quite doing it, you can look for a LoRA that introduces that visual effect. You add it to the workflow and choose the weight (how much itll affect), and also use its tags if it has any. That way you can mix and match many visual aspects and character influences as you please

Comfy can look complicated. But its really just a bunch of connected nodes.
The basic thing is Load Checkpoint > Lora (if youre using) > Positive and Negative prompts> Ksampler > VAE decode > save image.

On a 5080 it'll run great.

comments.author: Karfman
comments.body:
You’re literally burning your own market segment here. By letting every random guy throw some quickly cobbled-together titles onto Steam, you’re collectively ensuring that nobody wants to drink from this poisoned well.

Using the very same customer base you ultimately want to reach as a live test study is just an incredibly dumb idea. Anyone with a single semester of business administration could tell you that, because it’s basic stuff.

The big misconception so many people here seem to have is that AI art is somehow the reason they fail in the market (because of “haters” or whatever). Larger studios get away with it much more easily because they don’t outsource core components of their concept. The average player probably does not care much whether a small swarm of agents debugged the code. But by now, the grifter bubble around this topic has generated such an immense backlash that most people are instantly put off when they see an obvious AI giveaway, like that piss-filter look or similar signs.

In the end, you’re doing exactly the same thing here, except apparently you’re even doing it deliberately to make some kind of point? I mean… hooray? A small test group could have told you that within ten minutes. Or, fine, use Itch.io. Instead, you’re cluttering Steam with it.

Maybe there really is a gem of a fun game hidden beneath the weird titles. The problem is that nobody will find it. It’s the same principle as with AI books or AI Etsy shops, you can't flood the market with subpar stuff  and wonder why people get annoyed. 

TLDR:

Stop throwing quantity over quality onto the actual market. There are other places for this, where nobody has a problem with small free experiments floating around. But the kind of market dilution that is increasingly happening here turns consumers against you. At the end of the day, it really is not more complicated than that, even if a lot of people here like to convince themselves otherwise.

If someone made a genuinely competent Dungeon Keeper-like using AI assets, for example, it would probably sell like hotcakes after the initial skepticism. The emphasis, however, is on *competent*. Twenty titles generated in the evenings after work over the course of a month will just get you pitchforks and torches. It really is not that hard to understand.

replies.author: Karfman
replies.body:
What kind of shadowboxing is this? The argument was never against AI art. It was against deliberately diluting your own market with subpar products. The filter example was only meant to illustrate that problem.

The issue was not originally the visual style itself. It was the sheer amount of low-quality content flooding every channel with that distinctive look, which poisoned the well for it. You have already reached a point where any resemblance to that style may put off potential customers, but it is not beyond recovery... yet.

Keep flooding Steam with this stuff, though, and there will eventually be a witch hunt. Rightfully so, because this approach makes the indie market worse for everyone involved. Take OP as an example: for the sake of this “experiment”, he created two similar games instead of one game that would probably have been better. In such a niche market, paying customers should not be the target audience for experiments like that. That was the whole point. And again, this is basic economics. As a small developer, you do not have the market power or customer loyalty to get away with this. That is why I said you are, in a sense, poisoning your own well.
